title: Build your portfolio
desc: GitHub, pitch deck, and showcase prep
content_html:
What You'll Do

In this project you'll take something you've already built in this programme — a chatbot, a game, an image classifier, a website, any AI-powered creation — and turn it into a professional, shareable portfolio piece. You'll publish it on GitHub with a clear README, design a short pitch deck that explains it to a non-technical audience, and rehearse a two-minute "showcase pitch" you could give at a demo day, to an employer, or to family and friends.

This isn't about learning to code from scratch — it's about the presentation, documentation and storytelling skills around work you've already done. By the end you'll have a live GitHub link, a polished slide deck, and the confidence to explain your project out loud in under two minutes.

What You'll Need

  • GitHub (github.com) — free, with unlimited public repositories. You'll need a working email to sign up. Not comfortable with the command line? GitHub Desktop (desktop.github.com) makes uploads easy.
  • A pitch-deck tool — Gamma (gamma.app, free AI credits for a deck or two) or Google Slides (slides.google.com) as a free, unlimited backup.
  • A chatbot — ChatGPT (chat.openai.com) or Claude (claude.ai) — to draft your README and pitch script.
  • Good to know: set up your GitHub and Gamma accounts early — email verification and sign-ups can eat your time.

Steps

  1. Warm up: why do employers and universities look at GitHub profiles and pitch decks instead of just asking you to describe your project? Note a couple of reasons.
  2. Create (or open) your GitHub account. Use a professional username — not a nickname — and add a simple photo or avatar.
  3. Make a new public repository named after your project (e.g. swahili-chatbot, trash-sorter-ai). Upload your existing files with "Add file → Upload files."
  4. Write a README. Start with this prompt in ChatGPT or Claude: "I built a project called [NAME]. It does [WHAT IT DOES] using [TOOLS/AI]. Write a clear, friendly GitHub README with: Project Title, Description, How It Works, Tools Used, What I Learned, Future Improvements."
  5. Read it critically and edit at least three sentences so it sounds like you and describes what you actually built — not what the AI assumed.
  6. Paste the final README into your repo's README.md using GitHub's web editor and commit it with a message like "Add project README."
  7. Now the pitch deck. The classic shape is: Problem → Solution → How It Works → Demo/Screenshot → What I Learned → What's Next.
  8. In Gamma (or Slides), try: "Create a 6-slide pitch deck for a project called [NAME] that solves [PROBLEM] using AI: a title slide, problem, solution, how-it-works, results/demo, and next-steps. Keep text short and the style clean and modern."
  9. Replace any placeholder images with real screenshots of your own project (your code, a chat, your app screen).
  10. Edit the slide text to cut AI filler and add real details and numbers ("tested with 20 sample sentences," not "tested extensively").
  11. Rehearse your two-minute pitch to a partner using only the slides as a visual aid — don't read off them. Get two bits of feedback: one thing that was clear, one that could be clearer or shorter.
  12. Revise, then do a final run timed to under two minutes.

Examples to Try

  • Chatbot project: a repo kiswahili-helper-bot whose README covers the problem (practising Swahili vocab), the tools used, and a "What I Learned" note about prompt design. Its deck has a bot-icon title slide, a classroom problem slide, a real chat screenshot, and two future features (voice input, more vocab).
  • Image classifier: trash-sorter-ai with a README explaining how it sorts recyclable vs non-recyclable items, plus a table of accuracy results. The deck has a "before AI / after AI" slide and a grid of five classifications — three right, two wrong — with an honest note on limitations.
  • Game project: ai-trivia-game with "How to Play" instructions and credit to any AI used. The deck opens with a bold problem ("Studying for exams is boring"), shows gameplay, and ends with a roadmap slide proposing a leaderboard.

Tips

  • Don't paste the AI's README or deck word-for-word. Ask yourself "is this really how I'd say it?" Making it yours is the main skill here.
  • Use real screenshots and real numbers — placeholder examples make your work look generic and untrustworthy.
  • GitHub setup runs long the first time — do account creation and email verification before you start the real work.
  • Gamma credits run out? Switch straight to Google Slides with the same 6-slide outline.
  • Project incomplete or lost? Build the portfolio around whatever you have — the skill is presentation, not perfection.

Think About It

  • What's the difference between a README and a pitch deck — why might you want both?
  • When the AI wrote your README or deck, what did it get right, and what was too generic?
  • Why use your own screenshots and numbers instead of AI placeholders?
  • If an employer saw only your GitHub repo, what would they learn about you as a builder?
  • How is pitching to a person different from describing a project in writing — what can a live pitch do that a README can't?

Challenge Yourself

  • Easy: Add a license file and a GitHub "badge" or two (e.g. "Made with Python," "Status: In Progress").
  • Medium: Record a 30–60 second screen or phone video demoing your project, upload it, and link it in your README and deck.
  • Hard: Deploy a live, clickable version of your project with a free hosting tool and add the link to your README and final slide, so anyone can try it without installing anything.
